Alan García (Latin American; 23 May 1949 - 17 April 2019) was a Peruvian politician who served as President of Peru for two non-consecutive terms, from 1985 to 1990 and from 2006 to 2011.

Ancient Israel and Judah were two Israelite kingdoms that existed in the Southern Levant during the Iron Age.

Grand Duchess Tatiana Nikolaevna of Russia

A former SAS trooper turned wilderness-TV host, in 2009 he became the Scout Association's youngest-ever Chief Scout at age 35 — who is this British adventurer?
Bear Grylls (born 7 June 1974) is a British adventurer, television presenter and former SAS trooper.

Before founding the party Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam and becoming chief minister of Tamil Nadu in 2026, this man was one of India's highest-paid Tamil cinema stars — making his leading debut in a 1992 film directed by his own father. Who is he?
C. Joseph Vijay (born 22 June 1974) is an Indian politician and former actor who is currently serving as the ninth chief minister of Tamil Nadu since May 2026.
Nicknamed the 'Father-in-law of Europe' for marrying his children into so many royal houses, which Danish king reigned from 1863 to 1906?
Christian IX (8 April 1818 - 29 January 1906) was King of Denmark from 15 November 1863 until his death in 1906.
This American anthropologist and anarchist gave the Occupy movement a leading voice and wrote provocative books like Debt: The First 5,000 Years and Bullshit Jobs — who was he?
David Graeber (February 12, 1961 - September 2, 2020) was an American anthropologist and anarchist social and political activist.
Often called the greatest jurist of the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras, this English barrister rose from the Inner Temple to Speaker of the House of Commons and Attorney General. Who was he?
Edward Coke (CUUK, formerly; 1 February 1552 - 3 September 1634) was an English barrister, judge, and politician.
Ascending to the Iraqi throne at age three after his father's death, this monarch was killed in the 1958 coup that ended the Hashemite monarchy — who is he?
Faisal II (2 May 1935 - 14 July 1958) was the last King of Iraq.

An Egyptian military revolutionary seized power in 1954, introduced sweeping land reforms, and became a hero across the Arab world by nationalizing a crucial waterway. Who led Egypt as its second president for sixteen transformative years?
Gamal Abdel Nasser (15 January 1918 - 28 September 1970) was an Egyptian military officer and revolutionary who served as the second president of Egypt from 1954 until his death in 1970.
This art-collecting Russian general and patron helped install Catherine the Great on the throne before his infidelities cost him his influence — who is he?
Grigory Orlov (17 October 1734 - 24 April 1783) was a Russian general and patron of arts who was Prince of the Holy Roman Empire (1772) and a favourite of Empress Catherine the Great.
House speaker, secretary of state, and a three-time loser of the presidency, this Kentuckian earned the nickname 'the Great Compromiser' for defusing sectional crises — who was he?
Henry Clay (April 12, 1777 - June 29, 1852) was an American lawyer, statesman, and diplomat who represented Kentucky in both the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate.
Son of a former prime minister, this Cambodian leader rose through the Royal Cambodian Army to deputy commander-in-chief before taking his father's job in 2023 — who is he?

Hun Manet (born 20 October 1977) is a Cambodian politician and military officer who has served as Prime Minister of Cambodia and Vice President of the ruling Cambodian People's Party (CPP) since 2023.
This mid-1740s bid to restore the exiled Stuarts to the British throne began in the Scottish Highlands and ended when its army turned back from Derby in December — which rebellion?
Jacobite rising of 1745 was an attempt to regain the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart.

This German-American newspaper editor and orator popularized 'propaganda of the deed' in the United States and was jailed several times after publishing literature on how to build and use bombs — who was he?
Johann Most (February 5, 1846 - March 17, 1906) was a German-American Social Democratic and then anarchist politician, newspaper editor, and orator.
This Indian politician has served since 2024 as both Minister of Communications and Minister of Development of the North Eastern Region — who is he?
Jyotiraditya Scindia (born 1 January 1971; Hindi) is an Indian politician who is serving as the 43rd Minister of Communications and 10th Minister of Development of North Eastern Region since 2024.

Co-recipient with the United Nations of the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize, this Ghanaian diplomat served as the organization's seventh secretary-general and later chaired an international group founded by Nelson Mandela — who was he?
Kofi Annan (8 April 1938 - 18 August 2018) was a Ghanaian diplomat and statesman who served as the seventh secretary-general of the United Nations from 1997 to 2006.
Once seen as Mao Zedong's likely successor, this Chinese politician served as head of state from 1959 until he was purged during the Cultural Revolution — who was he?
Liu Shaoqi (24 November 1898 - 12 November 1969) was a Chinese revolutionary and politician.
Orphaned of his father at three, this Roman emperor became the last of the Five Good Emperors and is remembered as much for his Stoic philosophy as his reign — who was he?
Marcus Aurelius (26 April 121 - 17 March 180) was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher.
Said to have lived 969 years — the longest recorded lifespan in the Bible — this patriarch was the grandfather of Noah — who is he?
Methuselah was a biblical patriarch and a figure in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
Possibly Arthur's own son in early Welsh tradition, this Arthurian figure was later recast as a treacherous nephew associated with the fateful Battle of Camlann. Who is he?
Mordred (or) is a major figure in the legend of King Arthur.
Born at Tsarskoye Selo and widely thought ill-prepared to rule, this monarch led his empire into World War I before abdicating in 1917 — and in 1918 his whole family was murdered. Who was he?
Nicholas II was Emperor of Russia from 1894 to 1917.
Once Britain's youngest sitting MP, this baronet drifted from the Conservatives to Labour before founding the British Union of Fascists in 1932 — who is it?
Oswald Mosley (16 November 1896 - 3 December 1980), was a British politician who rose to fame during the 1920s and 1930s when, disillusioned with mainstream politics, he turned to fascism.
This longtime CPI(M) state secretary became Kerala's 12th Chief Minister in 2016 and later served as Leader of the Opposition — who is he?
Pinarayi Vijayan (born 24 May 1945) is an Indian politician who served as the 12th Chief Minister of Kerala from 25 May 2016 to 18 May 2026.
Charged with murder after a deadly 1992 standoff with federal agents at his Idaho cabin, this self-proclaimed separatist was ultimately acquitted of most charges — who is he?
Randy Weaver (January 3, 1948 - May 11, 2022) was an American survivalist and self-proclaimed white separatist.
He was the longest-serving commandant of Auschwitz, in charge across two stretches between 1940 and 1945 — what was his name?
Rudolf Höss (also H, Hoe, or Hoess; 25 November 1901 - 16 April 1947) was a German SS officer and the commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
Briefly governor of Moscow Oblast in 2012, this member of Putin's inner circle led Russia's defence ministry until 2024, when he moved to secretary of the Security Council — who is he?
Sergei Shoigu (born 21 May 1955) is a Russian politician and military officer who has served as secretary of the Security Council since 2024.
Gaining wide use in American political discourse of the 1930s and '40s, this doctrine holds that governing authority carries some legitimacy, standing opposed to anarchism — what's it called?
Statism (from French, tat 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.
Before he became the Supreme Court's first African-American justice, this lawyer won 29 of the 32 civil rights cases he argued there, capped by 1954's Brown v. Board of Education — who is he?
Thurgood Marshall (July 2, 1908 - January 24, 1993) was an American lawyer who served as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States from 1967 until 1991.
Spanning roughly 800 to 1050 CE, this era saw Scandinavian raiders, traders, and settlers push across Europe and reach as far as North America — which age?

Viking Age (about 800-1050 CE) was the period during the Middle Ages when Norsemen known as Vikings undertook large-scale raiding, colonising, conquest, and trading throughout Europe and reached North America.
Starting in his father's grocery business at fifteen, this English industrialist built an empire on Sunlight Soap, Lux, and Lifebuoy. Who was he?

Traditionally chanted by a muezzin from a mosque's minaret before each of the five daily prayers, what is this Islamic call known as?
Adhan: Islamic call to prayer. The five prayer times are known in Arabic as fajr (فجر), dhuhr (ظهر), asr (عصر), maghrib (مغرب), and isha (عشاء).

Anne Boleyn: Queen of England from 1533 to 1536.

Assassination of Uthman: 656 murder of the third Rashidun caliph in Medina.

Battle of Alesia: Part of the Gallic Wars.
Born to King Shantanu and the river goddess Ganga, this Mahabharata hero renounced the throne and vowed lifelong celibacy so his father could marry Satyavati — who was he?

Ceres (mythology): Roman goddess of agriculture. In ancient Roman religion, Ceres ( SEER-eez, Latin: [ˈkɛreːs]) was a goddess of agriculture, grain crops, fertility, and motherly relationships.

A West Virginia farm boy who started WWII as an Army private and aircraft mechanic before becoming a flying ace, in October 1947 he became the first pilot confirmed to break the sound barrier in level flight — who was he?
Chuck Yeager: American flying ace and test pilot (1923–2020)

Marching his 13th Legion over a forbidden river into Italy in January 49 BC, Julius Caesar defied the Senate and triggered a civil war that made him dictator for life — this act gave its name to what idiom for a point of no return?
Crossing the Rubicon: Idiom meaning a point of no return. Caesar was not allowed to command an army within Italy proper, and by crossing the river with his forces was defying law and risking death.
Bribed by Philistine lords to learn the secret of a mighty Nazirite's strength, this biblical woman finally coaxed out the truth about his hair — who is she?
Delilah: Woman in the Book of Judges of the Hebrew Bible.

Duchy of Burgundy: Vassal territory of France, 918–1482.

Elaine Chao: American businesswoman and government official (born 1953)

Ethan Allen: American farmer, military officer and politician (1738–1789)

Gerhard Schröder: Chancellor of Germany from 1998 to 2005. Gerhard Fritz Kurt "Gerd" Schröder (born 7 April 1944) is a German former politician and lobbyist who served as Chancellor of Germany from 1998 to 2005.
According to Arthurian legend, this queen of Great Britain was famously seduced by Mordred during his rebellion against her husband, King Arthur — who is she?
Guinevere: Arthurian legend character. Guinevere has continued to be a popular character featured in numerous adaptations of the legend since the 19th-century Arthurian revival.

Harrison Schmitt: American politician and astronaut (born 1935)
The first practicing Orthodox Jew to head Israeli military intelligence, this retired general later served as IDF Chief of General Staff from January 2023 to March 2025. Who is he?

Juno (mythology): Ancient Roman goddess of marriage and childbirth.
She became the first female prime minister of Bangladesh — and only the second in the Muslim world after Benazir Bhutto — leading the country across two stints — who was she?
Khaleda Zia: Prime Minister of Bangladesh (1991–1996; 2001–2006)
Assassinated by the SS during the Night of the Long Knives in 1934, this German officer had served as the second-to-last chancellor of the Weimar Republic — who was he?
Kurt von Schleicher: Chancellor of Germany from 1932 to 1933.
So central was this late-Qing statesman to China's foreign affairs that the world dubbed him the "Oriental Bismarck" — who founded the Beiyang Fleet and led the Self-Strengthening Movement?
Li Hongzhang: Chinese statesman and general (1823–1901)
This Spanish expedition's captain made the first recorded European passage through the strait separating mainland Australia from New Guinea — a strait that now bears his name — who was he?
Luís Vaz de Torres: 16th- and 17th-century Galician maritime explorer.
Described in both the Bible and the Quran, this edible substance was said to have been provided by God to sustain the Israelites during their 40 years wandering the desert — what was it?
Manna: Edible substance described in the Bible.
Forged by Joseph Stalin from Bolshevik roots, this ideology ruled the Soviet Union and still underpins the governments of China, Cuba, Laos, and Vietnam — what is it called?

Named after its most prominent site and stimulated by contact with Minoan Crete, this Bronze Age mainland civilization built palatial states from roughly 1750 to 1050 BC — what's it called?
Mycenaean Greece: Late Bronze Age Greek civilization.
A former bus driver turned union leader, he served as Hugo Chávez's vice president before taking the top job in Venezuela in 2013 — who is he?
Nicolás Maduro: President of Venezuela from 2013 to 2026.
Spelling out as Na-Ma-Shi-Va-Ya, this five-syllable Hindu mantra is the most important in Shaivism and offers salutations to 'the auspicious one' — what is it?
Om Namah Shivaya: Hindu mantra. Om Namah Shivaya (Devanagari: ॐ नमः शिवाय; IAST: Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya) is one of the most popular Hindu mantras and the most important mantra in Shaivism.

At 93, this Cameroonian head of state is the world's oldest sitting president and the second-longest-ruling leader in Africa, having taken power in 1982 after his predecessor's surprise resignation — who is he?
Paul Biya: President of Cameroon since 1982.
Named the first viceroy of Italian East Africa, this general commanded Italian forces in both world wars and became Prime Minister after Fascism fell — who was he?
Nicknamed after a judge was told to tremble before God's authority by their founder, members of this group call each other Friends and reject creeds and hierarchical structures — which movement?
A central tenet of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, this idea holds that an immortal soul never disperses at death but passes into a newborn baby or an animal. What's the concept?

Notorious for humiliating defendants and handing down frequent death sentences, this German judge presided over the People's Court from 1942 to 1945 — who is he?
Nicknamed "Sam Bahadur" — the Brave — and a Military Cross winner in WWII, he led India's army during the 1971 war with Pakistan and became the country's first field marshal. Which general was he?
Founded in 312 BC by one of Alexander the Great's generals, this Hellenistic Greek state stretched from Anatolia to Afghanistan before Pompey folded it into Rome — which state was it?
Seleucid Empire: Hellenistic state in West Asia (312–63 BC)

Based on the island of Sumatra, this maritime empire became a key center for spreading Buddhism across Southeast Asia between the 7th and 11th centuries — which empire?
Srivijaya: Empire based on Sumatra (c. 671–1025 AD)

This branch of Marxism-Leninism is named for the Russian revolutionary who developed it alongside the Left Opposition and the Fourth International — what's it called?
Trotskyism: Variety of Marxism developed by Leon Trotsky.
Born in Turin, this ruler of Sardinia became the first king of a united Italy in 1861 and earned a nickname echoing an ancient Roman imperial title, 'Father of the Fatherland.' Who was he?
Victor Emmanuel II: King of Italy from 1861 to 1878.
Nicknamed the "Land Cruiser War," this conflict erupted in Sudan in 2003 and led to President Omar al-Bashir being indicted for genocide by the International Criminal Court. What was it?
War in Darfur: Genocidal conflict in Western Sudan.

Windsor Castle: Official country residence of British monarch.

Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was J. Robert Oppenheimer born?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Archimedes die?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.

Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-57 from?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russia. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.
Who is credited with discovering Aspirin?
Aspirin: Raffaele Piria. Aspirin is used to treat inflammatory conditions including Kawasaki disease, pericarditis, and rheumatic fever.
Who is credited with discovering Boron?
Boron: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.

The active component of vinegar and the second simplest carboxylic acid, this colourless liquid with the formula CH₃COOH has been produced in large quantities since the third millennium BCE. What is this acid?
Acetic acid is an acidic, colourless liquid and organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH (also written as CH3CO2H, C2H4O2, or HC2H3O2).
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.
What term describes the discipline of measuring human body dimensions, applied everywhere from ergonomics and architecture to tracking historical living standards?
Anthropometry (from Ancient Greek (nthrpos) 'human' and (mtron) 'measure') refers to the measurement of the human individual.

Distinguished from celestial mechanics by asking what heavenly bodies ARE rather than where they are, this science applies physics and chemistry to the Sun, stars, galaxies, and exoplanets — which discipline?
Astrophysics is a science that applies the methods and principles of physics and chemistry in the study of astronomical objects and phenomena including the universe.
This steroid medication treats conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis to asthma, and is also given before preterm birth to help speed a baby's lung development — what drug is it?
Betamethasone is a steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.

Derived from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart', this medical term describes a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes a red flag, sometimes just a sign of a well-conditioned athlete. Name the condition?
Bradycardia (brads), meaning "slow", and (karda), meaning "heart", also called bradyarrhythmia, is a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute (BPM).
Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on the region, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere — what is it?
Cougar (Puma concolor), also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large feline native to the Americas.
Caused by either too little insulin or cells that ignore it, this condition keeps blood sugar stubbornly high and comes chiefly in a type 1 and a type 2 — what is it?
Diabetes is a group of common endocrine diseases characterized by sustained high blood sugar levels.
This social science examines the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, analyzing everything from individual agents to entire economies. What discipline is this?
Economics is a social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services.
This class of mental health condition is defined by an enduring, pervasive pattern of behavior, emotion, and thought that deviates from social norms and develops early in life. What is it?
Erythritol is an organic compound, the naturally occurring achiral meso four-carbon sugar alcohol (or polyol).
Which evergreen conifer genus has needle-like leaves attached singly to the branch by a circular base, and cones that stand upright like a cedar's rather than hanging down? What is it?
Fir are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.

These common coastal seabirds, most closely related to terns and skimmers, were once known by an older name still surviving in some English dialects and cognate with the German word Möwe — what birds are they?
Gull (see Taxonomy), are seabirds of the subfamily Larinae.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Reclassified in 2021 as part of the order Psocodea alongside booklice and barklice, these tiny wingless parasites cement their eggs to a single host for life — what are they called?
Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Google's employee No. 20 and its first woman software engineer, she later left to run a famous internet company as CEO from 2012 until Verizon bought it — who is she?
Marissa Mayer (born May 30, 1975) is an American business executive, software engineer, and investor who served as president and chief executive officer of Yahoo!
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With somewhere between 66 and 70 species across nine subfamilies, this carnivore family stretches from tiny weasels all the way up to the wolverine. What is it?
Mustelidae (from Latin mustela, weasel) are a diverse family of carnivoran mammals, including weasels, badgers, otters, sea otters, polecats, martens, grisons and wolverines.

Considered primary if a child has never had a long dry stretch, this common childhood condition — usually a developmental delay rather than an illness — is commonly called bedwetting. What's its clinical name?
Nocturnal enuresis (NE), also informally called bedwetting, is involuntary urination while asleep after the age at which bladder control usually begins.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this unit of mass equals 1/16 of a pound in its common form, though a heavier 'troy' version weighs precious metals — name the unit?
Ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.

This short-acting barbiturate is used as a sedative and anticonvulsant in low doses, but in high doses causes fatal respiratory arrest, making it a drug of choice for both veterinary euthanasia and U.S. executions — what is it?
Pentobarbital (US) or pentobarbitone (British and Australian) is a short-acting barbiturate typically used as a sedative, a preanesthetic, and to control convulsions in emergencies.
Native to Eurasia and identifiable by short, blue-green needles, this member of the pine family goes by several regional common names — name the species (Latin binomial)?
Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Split into the strepsirrhines — lemurs and lorisids — and the haplorhines — tarsiers, monkeys and apes — this order ranges in size down to tiny Madame Berthe's — what is it?

Primate is an order of mammals, which is further divided into the strepsirrhines, which include lemurs, galagos, and lorisids; and the haplorhines, which include tarsiers and simians (monkeys and apes).

Founding an organization promoting swadeshi economics against globalization, this Indian social activist later allied with a yoga guru to combine that economic message with the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda — who is he?
Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 - 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.

This English X-ray crystallographer's photographs were crucial to unraveling the structure of DNA, yet her contribution went largely unrecognized in her lifetime, earning her posthumous nicknames like "the wronged heroine" — who was she?
Rosalind Franklin (25 July 1920 - 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Once placed alone in the genus Uncia before phylogenetics moved it into Panthera, this high-altitude cat ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas — what is it?
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a species of large cat in the genus Panthera of the family Felidae.
Lacking the powder down that herons and ibises use to clean off fish slime, these bill-clattering wading birds come in 20 living species across six genera — which birds?
Stork are large, long-legged, long-necked wading birds with long, stout bills.

Equal to one weber per square metre, this SI unit of magnetic flux density was adopted in 1960 and named for a Serbian-American electrical engineer, on the proposal of a Slovenian engineer — name this unit?
Tesla (unit) (symbol: T) is the unit of magnetic flux density (B) (also called magnetic B-field) in the International System of Units (SI).
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Known by the common name yarrow, this pungent, fernleaved plant in the daisy family is used in traditional medicine and as livestock feed — what is its scientific name?
Achillea millefolium: Species of plant. Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
A former IMF economist, this politician has served as President of Ivory Coast since 2010 after earlier stints as the country's prime minister in the early 1990s — who is he?
Alassane Ouattara: President of Ivory Coast since 2010. Ouattara became the president of the Rally of the Republicans (RDR), an Ivorian political party, in 1999.
Also known as shadbush, serviceberry, or juneberry, this rose-family shrub's berries inspired the name of a Canadian city — which genus?
First described by a German entomologist in 1818 and known as the 'marsh mosquito,' this genus is the only one that transmits malaria to humans — which genus is it?
Anopheles: Genus of mosquito. The genus Anopheles diverged from other mosquitoes approximately 100 million years ago (mya), and, like other mosquitoes, the eggs, larvae, and pupae are aquatic.
The third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere at nearly 1%, this noble gas takes its name from an Ancient Greek word meaning 'lazy' or 'inactive' — what element is it?
Argon: Chemical element with atomic number 18 (Ar)
Native to the Americas and prized for thousands of years for its unusually oily fruit, this evergreen of the laurel family bears what's botanically a giant berry around a single seed — what is it?
Avocado: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family.
Nicknamed 'top shelf' dizziness, this inner-ear disorder causes brief spinning sensations lasting under a minute whenever you tilt or turn your head — what is this condition called?
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: Medical condition. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), sometimes called "top shelf vertigo", is a disorder arising from a problem in the inner ear.
Composed of plasma plus red cells, white cells, and platelets, this circulatory fluid delivers oxygen and nutrients to the body while carrying away waste — what is it?
Blood: Body fluid in the circulatory system. Plasma, which constitutes 55% of blood fluid, is mostly water (92% by volume), and contains proteins, glucose, mineral ions, and hormones.
Grown on one of the Amazon's largest and longest-lived trees, this selenium-rich edible seed comes in a shell weighing up to 2 kilograms combined with its fruit. What is it?
Brazil nut: Species of tree and its edible seeds.
Native to tropical Africa, this gourd-producing vine yields fruit that can be eaten young as a vegetable or dried and hollowed out into bowls, ladles, or even musical instruments — what is it?
Calabash: Species of bottle gourd plant.
Ranked the world's richest person by Forbes from 2010 to 2013, this Mexican tycoon built his fortune largely through telecommunications and remains Latin America's wealthiest individual — who is he?
Around 20 millimetres long with a shimmering structural-green shell and a coppery underside, this beetle is identified by its isosceles-triangle scutellum — which species?
Cetonia aurata: Species of beetle. The scutellum is the small V-shaped area between the wing cases; it may show several small, irregular, white lines and marks.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Named for an Indonesian island where an 18th-century naturalist first catalogued it, this pungent, oregano-scented succulent also goes by Cuban oregano and Indian borage — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus: Species of plant. Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Latin for 'raven,' this widely distributed bird genus includes crows and rooks and gave a group of its members the eerie collective noun 'a murder' — what genus is it?
Corvus: Genus of birds including crows, ravens and rooks.

First synthesized in 1874, this insecticide earned its discoverer a 1948 Nobel Prize and was used in WWII against malaria and typhus before becoming infamous for its environmental damage — what is it?
DDT: Organochloride known as an insecticide.

This group of microalgae generates roughly a fifth to a half of Earth's oxygen each year, and its dead shells drift on Saharan winds to fertilize the entire Amazon basin with millions of tons of dust annually. What are they?
Diatom: Single-celled alga with a silica cell wall.
The only living relative of the extinct Steller's sea cow, this seagrass-grazing marine mammal is most abundant in the waters of northern Australia — what is it?
Dugong: Species of marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees.
Co-founding Mattel with his wife Ruth, this inventor helped bring Barbie, Hot Wheels, and Chatty Cathy to toy shelves — who is he?
Elliot Handler: American inventor and business magnate (1916–2011)
Made by yeast fermenting sugars and once used as a general anesthetic, this colorless flammable liquid is the world's second most consumed drug, behind only caffeine — what is it?
Proposed in 1724 by a physicist who set water's freezing point at 32 degrees and boiling at 212, this temperature scale was originally anchored to a freezing brine solution — which scale?
Fahrenheit: Temperature scale. The Fahrenheit scale is a temperature scale based on one proposed in 1724 by the physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit (1686–1736).
Grown for both food and fiber, this plant's seeds are pressed into linseed oil while its stem fibers are woven into linen for sheets and clothing. What plant is it?
This Canadian physician and author has written five books linking childhood trauma to conditions like ADHD and addiction, though critics question the evidence behind some claims — who is he?
Caused by a genetic variant in the UGT1A1 gene, this harmless liver condition slows the breakdown of bilirubin and can trigger jaundice during stress, exercise, or fasting — what is it called?
Gilbert's syndrome: Medical condition. It is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and occasionally in an autosomal dominant pattern depending on the type of variant.

Despite its name, this marine reptile's shell ranges from olive to black — its nickname actually comes from the color of the fat beneath its carapace, built up from an all-plant diet — which species is this?
Green sea turtle: Species of large sea reptile. The dorsoventrally flattened body of C. mydas is covered by a large, teardrop-shaped carapace; it has a pair of large, paddle-like flippers.

Made by fusing heavy nuclei in tiny quantities, this superheavy element 108 has a special isotope whose "magic numbers" of protons and neutrons make its deformed nucleus unusually stable — what is it?
Hassium: Chemical element with atomic number 108 (Hs)
Its name means 'river horse' in Ancient Greek, yet this semiaquatic sub-Saharan giant — the largest even-toed ungulate alive — is more closely tied to pigs than to horses; what is it?
Hippopotamus: Species of large semi-aquatic mammal.
Marketed as Buscopan, this anticholinergic medication treats abdominal cramps, bladder and biliary spasms, and can ease respiratory secretions near the end of life — what drug is it?
Hyoscine butylbromide: Anticholinergic medication. It is also used to improve excessive respiratory secretions at the end of life.
An application of computer science, this field covers not just computers and networks but also distribution technologies like television and telephones — what is it?
Information technology: Computer-based technologies. Whisler commented that "the new technology does not yet have a single established name.
Sometimes called the founder of pneumatic chemistry, this 17th-century Brussels physician coined the word 'gas' and ran a famous five-year willow-tree experiment. Who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont: Chemist and physician (1580–1644)
Equal to the work done when a one-newton force moves an object one metre, this SI unit of energy is named for a 19th-century English physicist — which unit?
Joule: SI unit of energy. The joule ( JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI).
Named from a Norwegian word for 'small fry of fish,' these shrimp-like crustaceans form a biomass of some 379 million tonnes in the Southern Ocean alone — which creatures?

Krill: Small, shrimp-like crustaceans; order of crustaceans. Krill (Euphausiids) (sing.: krill) are small and exclusively marine crustaceans of the order Euphausiacea, found in all of the world's oceans.
Marked by weariness and a desire to act without the energy to do so, which condition can be a normal response to poor sleep or stress, or a sign of underlying illness?
Lethargy: State of tiredness, weariness, fatigue, or lack of energy.
Predominantly black and white with pink and grey highlights, this small Eurasian bird forms social flocks of six to seventeen outside breeding season and often nests in thorny scrub. What is it?
Long-tailed tit: Species of bird in Europe and Asia.
Domesticated some 9,000 years ago in southern Mexico from a wild grass called teosinte, this tall stout grain was once planted beside beans and squash in the Three Sisters trio — what is it?
Maize: Species of grass cultivated as a food crop.

Born from a US-UK cooperative effort begun in the early 1970s to improve on a first-generation jump jet, this vertical-takeoff-capable attack aircraft has served the US Marine Corps plus Spanish and Italian navies — which aircraft?
McDonnell Douglas AV-8B Harrier II: Anglo-American VSTOL ground-attack aircraft.
Sold under the brand name Medrol, this synthetic steroid can trigger iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome if not carefully tapered after high-dose use for acute flares — name the drug?
Its dust-like, colored, fuzzy appearance on food comes from spores, and its branching network of hyphae — called a mycelium — counts as a single organism; what fungal structure is this?
Mold: Wooly, dust-like fungal structure or substance.
Lacking a cell wall entirely, this genus of bacteria is naturally resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics that target cell-wall synthesis — which genus?
Mycoplasma: Genus of bacteria. Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.

Published in the Principia Mathematica, this principle holds that every particle in the cosmos attracts every other with a pull proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the squared distance between them — which principle is it?
Newton's law of universal gravitation: Classical statement of gravity as force.
First described by Linnaeus in 1758, this medium-sized spotted wild cat hunts armadillos and opossums at twilight across a range from the southwestern US to South America — what cat is it?
Ocelot: Species of wild cat. It is native to the southwestern United States, Mexico, Central and South America, and the Caribbean islands of Trinidad and Margarita.

Most members of this order of over 200 species are solitary night hunters with broad heads, binocular vision, and feathers tuned for silent flight — though oddballs like the burrowing kind break the mold. What are they?
Owl: Birds from the order Strigiformes.
Nicknamed the empress tree for its fast growth and showy foxglove-like blooms, which East Asian hardwood has become an invasive species across the Eastern US?
Paulownia tomentosa: Species of deciduous tree classified in its own family.
Its name combines the Greek words for 'love' and 'tree,' and with over 600 accepted species it's the second-largest genus in the arum family after Anthurium — which popular houseplant genus?
Caused by viral infections, autoimmune disorders, or pulmonary embolism, this condition inflames the membranes lining the lungs and chest cavity, causing sharp pain when breathing — which condition?
Pleurisy: Disease of the lungs. Pleurisy, also known as pleuritis, is inflammation of the membranes that surround the lungs and line the chest cavity (pleurae).
Caused by a single mutation in the LMNA gene, this rare disorder causes children to age dramatically faster than normal, with most not living past their twenties — which condition?
Progeria: Genetic disorder that causes early aging.
In Euclidean geometry, which fundamental relation says the square on a right triangle's longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two — famously written a² + b² = c²?
Pythagorean theorem: Relation between sides of a right triangle.
This biological process comes in two forms — asexual, as seen in cloning, and sexual, which combines gametes carrying half the usual chromosome count — what's the process called?
Reproduction: Biological process. Reproduction (or procreation or breeding) is the biological process by which new individual organisms – offspring – are produced from their parent or parents.
The second woman ever to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine — and the first American-born one — this physicist shared the 1977 award for developing the radioimmunoassay. Who was she?
Rosalyn Sussman Yalow: American medical physicist (1921–2011)

First used in English in the early 15th century and possibly named after a Mediterranean island, this term covers small oily forage fish under 15 centimeters, with larger ones called pilchards — what's the fish?
Sardine: Common name for various small, oily forage fish.
Domesticated more than 3,000 years ago and prized for having one of the highest oil contents of any seed, which crop is also known as benne?
Sesame: Plant cultivated for its edible seeds.

Once extracted from the ashes of certain salt-absorbing plants and now produced from ordinary salt and limestone via the Solvay process, this alkaline compound is also known as washing soda or soda ash — what is it?
Sodium carbonate: Chemical compound. Sodium carbonate (also known as washing soda, soda ash, sal soda, and soda crystals) is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2CO3 and its various hydrates.
Also known as asteroids for belonging to the class Asteroidea, this marine invertebrate typically has a central disc and five arms — what is it?
Starfish: Class of echinoderms, marine animal.
Despite the naming confusion with true yams, this starchy tuberous root actually belongs to the morning glory family and hails from tropical Ecuador — which crop?
Sweet potato: Species of edible plant.
Famously nicknamed 'white ants,' these wood-munching eusocial insects are actually genetically closer to cockroaches than they are to true ants — what are they?
Termite: Social insects related to cockroaches.
He joined Apple in 1998 to run worldwide operations and stepped up to the top job in 2011 when Steve Jobs resigned — which executive now leads the company?
Estimated to date back to the end of the Jurassic period roughly 156 million years ago, this fungal genus includes several species of truffles prized as culinary delicacies — which genus?
Tuber (fungus): Genus of fungi. Tuber is a genus in the fungal family Tuberaceae, with estimated molecular dating to the end of the Jurassic period (156 Mya).
The primary flavor compound in the vanilla bean, this phenolic aldehyde is now more often made synthetically than extracted from the real pod — what is it?
Vanillin: Chemical compound. Vanillin is an organic compound with the molecular formula C8H8O3.
Native to the Baltic, Black, and Caspian Sea basins, this large freshwater fish's range now stretches from the UK to western China — which species?
Wels catfish: Species of fish. It has been introduced to several countries in Western Europe, Mediterranean and Asia as a prized sport fish.
Following her husband's death, this Russian economist and activist vowed to carry on his opposition work and now chairs the Human Rights Foundation — who is she?
Yulia Navalnaya: Russian economist and political activist (born 1976)
What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
The symbol for oxygen is O. Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
The symbol for terbium is Tb. Terbium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tb and atomic number 65.

Jennifer Connelly: Jennifer Lynn Connelly (born December 12, 1970) is an American actress.
In what year was Phil Collins born?
Phil Collins: Philip David Charles Collins (born 30 January 1951) is an English singer, drummer, songwriter, record producer, and actor.
In what year was Matthew Perry born?
Matthew Perry: Matthew Langford Perry (August 19, 1969 – October 28, 2023) was an American and Canadian actor.
In what year was Margot Robbie born?
Margot Robbie: Margot Elise Robbie ( MAR-goh ROB-ee; born 2 July 1990) is an Australian actress and producer.

Will Ferrell: John William Ferrell (born July 16, 1967) is an American actor, comedian, writer, and producer.

Elizabeth Olsen: Elizabeth Chase Olsen (born February 16, 1989) is an American actress.

Paul Mescal: Paul Colm Michael Mescal ( MESS-kəl; born 2 February 1996) is an Irish actor.

Tony Curtis: In his later years, Curtis made numerous television appearances.
In what year did Sean Connery die?
